title: Good tidings of great joy (Luke 2:8–20)
hookLine: the angel to the shepherds: fear not, a savior is born
tomorrow: now let me go in peace

lines: WATCH OVER THE FLOCK BY NIGHT.
THE GLORY SHONE ROUND ABOUT THEM.
cards: Out in the fields near Bethlehem, a few shepherds are keeping watch over their flock by night. It's dark, and the job is mostly staying awake. Not people anyone would invite to a palace.

Not people the emperor's census was thinking about. Then, in the King James Bible: "the angel of the Lord came upon them, and the glory of the Lord shone round about them: and they were sore afraid." Sore afraid.
Terrified. The dark field suddenly blazing. And the angel's first words are ones Zechariah and Mary have already heard.

teach.b: "Fear not: for, behold, I bring you good tidings of great joy, which shall be to all people. For unto you is born this day in the city of David a Saviour, which is Christ the Lord." Every phrase is loaded.
Good tidings means good news, the very thing the word gospel names, coming to shepherds, about a baby. To all people: not just the important ones. This day: tonight, not someday.
And the sign isn't a palace or a crown: "Ye shall find the babe wrapped in swaddling clothes, lying in a manger."

teach.h: THE SIGN IS HOW ORDINARY HE IS.
teach.b: The sign is how ordinary he is.

teach.h: GLORY TO GOD IN THE HIGHEST.
teach.b: Then the sky fills with a multitude of angels praising God: "Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace, good will toward men." That line opens the Gloria, a hymn still sung in churches.
Compare Bibles and the end of the line varies: the King James says good will toward men; other translations say peace among people with whom God is pleased.
Then the shepherds do the simplest thing: "Let us now go even unto Bethlehem, and see." They find everything as they were told, spread the word, and people wonder at it.
Then a quiet line: "But Mary kept all these things, and pondered them in her heart."

teach.h: GOOD TIDINGS OF GREAT JOY, TO ALL PEOPLE.
teach.b: Both are ways of receiving good news. And the shepherds go back to the same sheep, glorifying and praising God as they go.

how: Christians read the shepherds' story at Christmas, and the angels' song lives on in the Gloria, sung or said in Sunday worship in some churches, and in Christmas carols.

o: one who announces good news, from the angel's own verb
an angel who sings glory to God in the highest
a shepherd who keeps watch over a flock by night

p: a baby lying in a manger

the same two words Zechariah and Mary heard.

games.q: you're a shepherd. an angel has just told you where to find a newborn savior. it's the middle of the night, and you have sheep. what do you do?
o: go to Bethlehem now and see.
send one person and stay with the flock.
games.why: "let us now go even unto Bethlehem, and see." they find everything as they were told, and tell everyone.

practice: Find one piece of good news that's actually true, a friend's recovery, a kindness you saw, a baby born, a small win, and sit with it for a moment the way Mary pondered.
Then picture the person who'd most like to hear it, someone surrounded by bad news lately, and imagine telling them the way the shepherds did, a little breathless, not polished.
If you pray, give thanks for it first; if not, simply enjoy it before you share it.

wordCard.voice: Evangelist. The English word that comes from the angel's own verb, to announce good news, first spoken to shepherds in a dark field.

orig.note: Greek: I announce good news. the verb behind the English word evangelist.

carryVoice: Your line: great joy for all people. Not just the important ones. Day five hundred nine.
